Consult Summary:
25-year-old woman with known peanut allergy and asthma developed rapid-onset upper-lip swelling, dyspnea, chest tightness, and dizziness ~30 min after eating prawn soup; clinician suspects anaphylaxis. Ambulance arranged, advised immediate antihistamine, and instructed ED assessment with follow-up for adrenaline auto-injector and allergy work-up.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Suspected anaphylaxis to prawn (possible new shellfish allergy)
- Onset: began ~30 min after ingesting prawn soup at ~19:00 today.
- Symptoms: progressive upper-lip swelling, sensation of throat closing, difficulty breathing, chest tightness, dizziness.
- Course: worsening during call.
- Pertinent positives: prior similar reaction 1 year ago after Chinese food; required hospital assessment at age 6 for severe reaction (per mother).
- Pertinent negatives: no antihistamine taken before call; no epinephrine auto-injector available.
- Impression: Likely IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.

Issue 2: Asthma
- Uses salbutamol inhaler (“blue” reliever); no preventer inhaler.
- No current wheeze assessed during teleconsult, but respiratory compromise possible during allergic episode.

Issue 3: Food allergies
- Documented peanut allergy since childhood.
- Now probable shellfish (prawn) allergy; needs formal confirmation.
- No regular antihistamine regimen in place.

Medications:
- Salbutamol inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Occasional antihistamines (specific agent/dose/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- Peanut (IgE-mediated reaction).
- Shellfish (prawn) – suspected, newly identified today.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.
- Childhood anaphylaxis to peanuts (inferred from hospitalization at age 6; conflict noted: exact trigger unclear).
- No other conditions reported.

Social History:
- Lives with mother (present at time of call). Smoking, alcohol, occupation not discussed.

Preventative History:
- Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- Teleconsult; no vitals taken.
- Patient-reported findings: upper-lip edema, subjective throat tightness, dyspnea, dizziness.
- Objective exam not possible via video.

Plan:
- Call 999 ambulance for emergency assessment of suspected anaphylaxis (completed during call).
- Take available oral antihistamine immediately while awaiting EMS.
- Remain with a responsible adult until help arrives.
- Emergency department management anticipated: airway support, intramuscular adrenaline, steroids, observation.
- Post-discharge: GP follow-up to 
  • prescribe adrenaline auto-injector(s) and provide training,
  • arrange formal allergy referral and testing (peanut, shellfish, others),
  • review asthma control and consider adding preventer inhaler,
  • supply regular non-sedating antihistamine as precaution.
- Advise patient to avoid prawn/shellfish and carry medical alert identification until assessed.
- Patient instructed to contact service after hospital discharge for ongoing management.

Quality checks (document_quality):

● Expected elements missing: comprehensive medication list (only reliever inhaler documented); current vitals; full allergy list confirmation; immunization status; smoking/alcohol history.
● Internal conflicts: unclear whether childhood hospitalization was for peanut reaction or other trigger.
● Transcript quality: clear dialogue; minor background noise but clinically adequate.
